explainers.title: The adjoint method gets the gradient of a loss through an ODE solve by integrating one more ODE backwards, and a finite-difference check proves it right
explainers.summary: To train a neural ODE you need the derivative of a loss with respect to the weights through the solver. The adjoint method gets it from a second ODE integrated backwards in time, with a memory cost that does not grow with the number of steps. Whatever way the gradient is obtained, it must be checked against central finite differences, whose error first falls and then rises with the step because of truncation and rounding.

explainers.title: A straight line on a 1000/T plot is an activation energy
explainers.summary: Reaction rates and ignition delays change by orders of magnitude with temperature. Plot the logarithm against 1000/T and an Arrhenius process becomes a straight line whose slope is the activation energy.

explainers.title: Semi-Lagrangian advection never blows up, but every step blurs: the interpolation is a hidden diffusion
explainers.summary: Stam's advection traces each cell back along the velocity and copies the value found there. It is stable for any time step because it only averages, but linear interpolation averages neighbours and so smears sharp features exactly like a diffusion with a known coefficient. MacCormack's correction removes most of the blur and a clamp keeps it from overshooting.

explainers.title: Jacobi iteration smooths the pressure but converges at a rate cos(pi/(N+1)): 6 to 24 sweeps are nowhere near a solve
explainers.summary: Jacobi replaces every pressure by the average of its neighbours corrected by the divergence. The error shrinks by the spectral radius of the iteration matrix each sweep, and for an N by N grid that is cos(pi/(N+1)): just below one, so thousands of sweeps are needed to solve and the 6 to 24 sweeps of the hero only smooth. Conjugate gradients, Gauss-Seidel with over-relaxation and multigrid change the rate; the residual plot of the Flow workspace shows the difference.

explainers.title: Incompressible flow: the velocity must have zero divergence, and the pressure is whatever enforces it
explainers.summary: Water and slow air do not compress, so the velocity field has zero divergence at every instant. Pressure has no equation of its own: it is the field whose gradient, subtracted from the velocity, removes whatever divergence the other terms create. Splitting a time step into 'move things around' and 'project onto the divergence-free fields' is the idea behind the home-page hero and behind the Flow workspace.

explainers.title: The projection solves one sparse matrix every step: minus four on the diagonal, plus one for each neighbour
explainers.summary: Finding the pressure that removes the divergence is a linear system A p = b. A is the five-point Laplacian: a row for each cell with minus the number of neighbours on the diagonal and plus one for each neighbour, so only five of n entries in a row are nonzero. Walls, open sides and obstacles change the rows at the edge, and a box with only walls makes A singular. The Matrix tab of the Flow workspace draws the real matrix.

explainers.title: Vorticity confinement and buoyancy are forces added by hand: the first puts back the curls the grid smears out, the second makes hot gas rise
explainers.summary: Numerical diffusion damps small vortices, so a simulated plume looks smoother than a real one. Fedkiw's vorticity confinement computes where the vorticity is concentrated and adds a force that pushes the flow around those places, with a strength set by one parameter. Buoyancy is a body force proportional to the temperature (and minus the weight of the smoke), the Boussinesq model. Both are cheap and visually effective, and both are modelling choices, not physics.

explainers.title: A potential energy surface is the electronic energy as a function of where the nuclei are
explainers.summary: Because nuclei are thousands of times heavier than electrons, one can solve the electrons for fixed nuclear positions and read the energy as a landscape. Minima are molecules, saddle points are transition states, and the height of a saddle sets a rate.

explainers.title: A gasifier is a ledger: balance the atoms, minimise the Gibbs energy, size the walls
explainers.summary: Gasification can be reasoned about with three tools: atom and energy balances that say what must add up, an equilibrium calculation that says where the chemistry wants to go, and heat-transfer resistances that say how big and how hot the hardware must be.

explainers.title: A solid can be stored as its skin, as a distance field, or as a grid, and each makes different operations easy
explainers.summary: A CAD kernel stores the boundary of a solid as faces, edges and vertices. A signed distance function stores the distance to the boundary at every point, which turns Boolean operations into min and max. Meshing then fills the solid with simple cells whose shape decides how good a simulation can be.

explainers.title: Making nonlinear dynamics look linear: Koopman lifts, snapshot fits (DMD) and low-dimensional modes (POD)
explainers.summary: A nonlinear system can sometimes be written exactly as a linear one in a bigger set of observables (a Koopman lift). Dynamic mode decomposition fits the best linear step map to snapshots by least squares, and proper orthogonal decomposition finds the few directions that carry most of the snapshot energy. Each is exact only when the chosen observables or modes are closed under the dynamics, so the honest check is a rollout from a new start.

explainers.title: A flame speed is set by reaction rate and diffusion: S_L scales as the square root of their product
explainers.summary: A premixed flame is a wave that heats the fresh gas by conduction until it reacts. Balancing the heating against the heat release gives the scaling S_L ~ sqrt(alpha times reaction rate), which explains the bell curve in equivalence ratio and the strain rate at which a flame dies.

explainers.title: A latent neural ODE learns the dynamics in a few coordinates: encode, evolve, decode, and check what was lost
explainers.summary: When many measured variables move together, a map from state to a few latent coordinates can carry the whole motion. A latent neural ODE encodes the state, evolves the latent vector with a small ODE and decodes back. It works when the latent subspace is closed under the dynamics and fails when it is not, or when a new start leaves the span of the training data: both can be measured with a reconstruction error and a latent-consistency error.

explainers.title: The shape of the loss decides how fast training goes: curvature, condition number and why optimizers behave differently
explainers.summary: Near a minimum a loss looks like a bowl whose curvatures are the eigenvalues of the Hessian. Gradient descent must keep its step below 2 over the largest curvature, so it crawls along the flattest direction; the ratio of largest to smallest curvature, the condition number, sets how many steps it needs. Momentum, preconditioning and rescaling the inputs all work by changing that ratio, and a slice through the landscape is the way to look at it.

explainers.title: At low Reynolds number flow is a parabola, mixing is diffusion, and curvature and particle size bring inertia back
explainers.summary: In a microchannel viscosity wins: the velocity profile is the Hagen-Poiseuille parabola, the pressure drop is linear in flow rate, and streams mix only by diffusion. Bend the channel and Dean vortices appear; add particles and inertial focusing places them on fixed lines.

explainers.title: Near any point a smooth map is a matrix, and its determinant is how much area it gains or loses
explainers.summary: A map sends every point of the plane to a new point and so deforms the whole plane. Zoomed in, the deformation is a matrix, the Jacobian. Its determinant is the local area scale factor and its sign says whether the plane was flipped, which is exactly the factor needed to change variables in an integral. Chains of maps multiply their Jacobians, and the stretch directions come from the Jacobian's singular values, not always from its eigenvalues.

explainers.title: A flame measured from video is a number with a ruler, a threshold and an interval
explainers.summary: Turning a flame video into millimetres takes four decisions: how many millimetres a pixel is, where the flame edge is, which statistic summarises the time series, and how wide an interval to report. Each decision has a formula and an error you can compute.

explainers.title: A neural ODE learns the rate law: the network is the right-hand side of dy/dt, and its picture is a vector field
explainers.summary: A rate law says how fast the state changes when the system is in a given state. A neural ODE replaces the unknown rate law with a network, trains it so that integrating it reproduces measured trajectories, and the learned function is drawn as a vector field. For mass-action kinetics the rate law is linear or polynomial in the concentrations, so the simplest learner is a regression on derivatives, and the same structure (conservation, positive rates) can be built into a network.

explainers.title: An optimizer is a way of walking a landscape, and the fair way to compare walkers is best-so-far against evaluations
explainers.summary: An objective function is a landscape. Gradient descent, Nelder-Mead and evolution strategies walk it in three different ways, each with a landscape it handles badly. Compare them by the best value found against the number of function evaluations on a log axis, and when two goals pull apart, report the Pareto front instead of one weighted number.

explainers.title: A power mean turns a loss into a dial between average and worst case, and scaling decides which variable owns the gradient
explainers.summary: When a model has several outputs, the loss must combine their errors into one number. The power mean with exponent p is a family: p = 1 is the average, p = 2 the root mean square, larger p approaches the maximum, and p near 0 the geometric mean. The exponent changes which component the gradient listens to, and so does the scale of each variable: an unscaled large variable can own the whole gradient.

explainers.title: Correlation is a tilted ellipse, and it decides how input uncertainty reaches the output
explainers.summary: Two uncertain inputs that move together are a tilted ellipse of possible values, and a Cholesky factor turns independent random numbers into exactly that cloud. A linear rule then says how much of the cloud's width reaches the output, Monte Carlo checks it with an error that shrinks only as one over the square root of the sample count, and Latin hypercube or Sobol designs place the same number of samples far more evenly than random draws.

explainers.title: Rounding the weights to a grid: step size, error bounds, and how the error travels through a network and a rollout
explainers.summary: Quantization replaces each weight by the nearest point of a grid with $2^b$ levels. The error of one weight is at most half a grid step, the error of a layer output grows like the square root of the number of inputs in practice and at worst linearly, and in a rollout it is shaped by the stability of the dynamics. Every extra bit halves the error, and a fair comparison fixes the bit budget and checks the whole rolled-out trajectory, not one step.

explainers.title: One-step loss can look perfect while the rollout drifts: training on longer horizons exposes the error that compounds
explainers.summary: A model of dy/dt can be trained by asking it to predict the next state from the true current one (one step, or teacher forcing) or by integrating it over many steps from the initial state and comparing the whole path (a rollout). A tiny error per step is invisible in the first loss but compounds in the second, and measurement noise can hide a systematic error that only a long horizon makes visible. A horizon curriculum starts short and grows.

explainers.title: A stiff system makes an explicit solver crawl, and a neural ODE has to learn that same right-hand side
explainers.summary: Stiffness means one very fast decaying mode forces an explicit method to take tiny steps long after that mode is gone. The step limit comes from the stability region of the method, implicit methods remove it, and an adaptive solver on a stiff problem ends up limited by stability rather than accuracy. A neural ODE learns the right-hand side from data, so its rollouts inherit both the stiffness and the growth of every small error in what it learned.

explainers.title: Turbulence is a cascade of eddies, and averaging it leaves a stress you have to model
explainers.summary: Energy enters a turbulent flow at large scales and is passed down to small ones, which is why the spectrum falls as k to the minus five thirds. Averaging the equations hides the eddies but leaves the Reynolds stress, and every closure is a way of guessing it.

explainers.title: Verification asks one question: does the error fall at the order the scheme promises?
explainers.summary: A solver is verified when its error shrinks at the theoretical rate as the grid is refined. The observed order, Richardson extrapolation, the grid convergence index and a manufactured solution are four tools for answering that, and none of them says whether the equations are the right ones.

explainers.title: A coupled-solver figure asks: did the two halves agree at their shared boundary, and did the iteration settle?
explainers.summary: Conjugate heat transfer and fluid-structure interaction solve two sets of equations that meet at an interface. The figures to read are the interface quantities (temperature, flux, displacement) and the convergence flag, because a plausible-looking field can be the product of an iteration that never finished.

explainers.title: An ignition figure asks one thing: when does the chemistry outrun the cooling, and does the kernel then sustain itself?
explainers.summary: A warm patch either cools back or runs away. The tell-tale is a sharp knee in the hottest-point curve while the domain average barely moves. Reading it means finding the knee, checking what the snapshots show on either side of it, and asking how much of the fuel the burning region has actually consumed.

explainers.title: Stochastic-equation figures ask two questions: does the ensemble match the exact statistics, and does the scheme converge as claimed?
explainers.summary: An SDE has two faces: individual noisy paths and the evolving probability density they sample. Each figure in this group tests one link between them. The reading skill is to separate the error due to the time step from the sampling error due to a finite number of paths.

explainers.title: Particle-model figures ask: does the stochastic model conserve what it must, and does it add the spread that the deterministic model lacks?
explainers.summary: Stochastic closures replace a single deterministic value with a distribution sampled by particles. The reading skill is to check first what the model must conserve (mean, energy balance), then what it is meant to add (spread, off-manifold scatter, backscatter), and to ask whether the sampling error is small enough to see the difference.

explainers.title: A mesh figure answers one question: are the cells the right size, in the right places, with the boundaries labelled?
explainers.summary: A structured mesh is a bookkeeping device: it fixes how many unknowns there are, how big each cell is, and where each boundary sits. Reading one means counting cells, checking spacing and boundary labels, and knowing what a coarser or finer version of the same mesh costs and buys.

explainers.title: Advection schemes: the same wave, four ways to be wrong
explainers.summary: Move a bump or a step across a grid with different spatial schemes and the shape that comes out shows the scheme's character: smeared by numerical diffusion, ringing from dispersion, blown up by instability, or kept bounded by a limiter.

explainers.title: Diffusion, meshes and Burgers: three small problems with a known answer
explainers.summary: A diffusion problem with an exact solution, a one-dimensional mesh with a stretching ratio, and a viscous Burgers wave that steepens into a shock: simple pictures for checking what time stepping, grid spacing and viscosity do to a solution.

explainers.title: Stability and dispersion plots: where in wavenumber or in the complex plane does the scheme fail?
explainers.summary: Von Neumann and stability-region figures replace a simulation by a function: the factor by which each wavelength is multiplied per step, or the set of values h times lambda a time integrator tolerates. Reading them predicts blow-up before running anything.

explainers.title: A geometry figure is a render of a shape, so the evidence of correctness is the number printed beside it, not the picture
explainers.summary: Three engines draw the same revolved nozzle, and four feature figures show revolve, fillet, shell and sweep on a signed-distance kernel. Renders of different correct kernels look alike, so read what each render is supposed to show, check it against the construction, and rely on printed volumes and watertightness for agreement.

explainers.title: Ignition is a runaway: heat released grows faster than heat lost, and the figure shows the moment the balance tips
explainers.summary: A key-frame strip plus a hot-spot temperature history shows a warm patch slowly warming, then jumping to flame temperature at a sharp tipping point. Read the history for when the tipping happens and the strip for what it does in space.

explainers.title: A design-sweep heatmap is only as informative as its colour scale, its caption and the question its metric answers
explainers.summary: A purity heatmap, a separation-resolution sweep and a velocity field in a stepped micro-channel are the three typical outputs of a microfluidic design study. Read the metric definition and the caption's own caveats before reading the colours: these figures state that the 2D model cannot produce the separation it is being asked about.

explainers.title: A validation figure compares a computed quantity with an exact or published law, and a miss that is shown is evidence too
explainers.summary: Pipe flow against the exact parabola, particle migration against the tubular-pinch equilibrium, and secondary-flow intensity against Dean's scaling are four checks of a low-Reynolds-number solver. Read each for what it is compared against, what the pass or miss label says, and what the footnote text adds.

explainers.title: A convergence plot asks one question: does the error fall at the rate the scheme promises?
explainers.summary: On a log-log plot the slope of error against grid spacing is the observed order of accuracy. A scheme counts as verified when that slope matches theory, so the whole job of this figure is to be compared with its reference slopes.

explainers.title: A multiphysics result figure must show that the physics is there, that the run converged, and what it was checked against
explainers.summary: Cavity flow, conjugate heat transfer, boiling, fluid-structure interaction and structural cantilever figures are panel sheets: fields, profiles and histories from one coupled run. Read each panel for what it can prove, and read the title and empty panels first, because several of these panels report that a run did not converge or that data were not available.

explainers.title: Before optimizing, check the three things it depends on: the model, the objective and the gradient
explainers.summary: A penalized-flow model, a dissipated-power identity and an analytic gradient checked against finite differences are the standard pre-flight tests of a density-based topology optimization. Each figure is a check with a pass criterion; read how large the discrepancy is, against what, and how it changes with the penalty and the mesh.

explainers.title: Stability figures ask whether an error mode grows or decays, and by how much per step
explainers.summary: Stability regions, amplification-factor curves, CFL sweeps and step-profile comparisons are four views of one idea: a numerical scheme multiplies each error mode by a factor every step. If that factor stays at or below one in size the run is stable; how far below one sets the numerical damping.

explainers.title: Stochastic figures compare random outputs with exact statistics, so read means, spreads and sample sizes, not single curves
explainers.summary: Sample paths against an exact mean and standard deviation, Monte Carlo error against sample size, an ensemble of mixing models and a randomized sub-grid viscosity are all pictures of distributions. The reading rule is the same: compare a statistic with its exact value, and ask how many samples stand behind each point.

explainers.title: Two bar charts, two questions: how much CO2 per unit heat, and does the flame stay inside the material limit?
explainers.summary: The CO2-intensity chart is a bookkeeping result: carbon in per kilojoule out. The peak-temperature chart is a constraint check against a dashed limit line. Read them together: the first says how far substitution helps, the second says whether the hardware survives it.

explainers.title: A mesh picture shows where the cells are, but not whether they are enough
explainers.summary: Mesh screenshots are evidence of effort, not of adequacy. Read them for where the resolution sits and where probe lines are placed, then ask for what the picture cannot show: cell counts, refinement ratio and the quantity that stopped changing.

explainers.title: A CFD geometry drawing is a contract: every labelled edge becomes a boundary condition
explainers.summary: Before a reacting-flow case can run, the domain has to be drawn, dimensioned and every edge named as an inlet, a wall or the reactor. Read these drawings as the list of what the solver will be told, and as a hint of where the flow will do something interesting: the sudden step where a narrow lance section opens into a wide reactor.

explainers.title: A labelled rig drawing links the hardware to the model: what stays, what is idealised
explainers.summary: A CAD view of a test rig is the bridge between the lab hardware and the simulation domain. Read it for the order of components along the flow path, then ask which parts the model keeps, which it replaces by a boundary condition and which it leaves out.

explainers.title: A design loop around an outside solver is read as an objective trace plus a constraint check
explainers.summary: Four figures show an optimiser driving external physics codes as black boxes: ignition delay with a temperature ceiling, rocket-nozzle thrust, and an airfoil lift coefficient. Each is read as a best-so-far trace against solver calls, then checked against the constraint and the design variables that matter.

explainers.title: A search trace shows where an optimiser looked; the surface is only the part you can draw honestly
explainers.summary: Height-map surfaces exist for exactly two inputs and one output. These figures show a CMA-ES search through the surface for two variables, through a coloured point cloud for three, and through a fixed slice for three: each is an honest answer to a different dimension problem.

explainers.title: A search benchmark has two axes: how low the energy goes, and how many evaluations it cost
explainers.summary: The four conformer-search figures compare a reinforcement-learning search with two reference methods on one molecule and one force field. Reading them means separating three things: the best energy found, the average quality of the policy's samples, and the evaluation count paid to get there.

explainers.title: A sample is only as good as its coverage: reading space-filling designs, dominance and propagated spread
explainers.summary: Three figures about what to do with samples: compare how evenly three samplers fill a box, extract the non-dominated points from a two-objective sample, and push input uncertainty through a response to see the output histogram. Each asks what the points are, not what the optimiser did.

explainers.title: A solver race is read on the convergence panel: how fast, how accurate, and on which landscape
explainers.summary: Two panels share one story. The left shows where each solver walked on a contour map; the right shows best-so-far objective against cumulative function evaluations on a log axis. The same five solvers on a smooth valley and on a multimodal field give different winners, which is the whole lesson.

explainers.title: In topology optimisation the gradient is the whole advantage, and the density picture shows why
explainers.summary: Two figures from one study: a convergence plot with a final bar chart, and the material layouts the three methods ended with. Together they show that a method that can use an exact gradient finds a structure, while methods that only see scores are still close to grey noise at the same cost.

explainers.title: A topology-optimisation picture is a load path: reading the project's vine mark
explainers.summary: The project's mark is the material layout from a compliance-minimising topology optimisation: a branching structure that carries a distributed load into a single support. Read as a structure, it shows where material is needed; as an emblem, it is a human choice of ink and typography.

explainers.title: A contact sheet is the cheapest instrument check: same camera, same scene, and a flame in every tile
explainers.summary: A grid of frames sampled at fixed intervals across a run lets you see, before trusting any measurement, that the camera did not move, the flame stayed in frame and the scale reference is visible. It also documents runs whose scale anchor is in doubt.

explainers.title: A detection overlay lets you check a measurement against the picture it came from
explainers.summary: Each overlay frame shows what the software decided is flame (green contour), where it put the centreline and tip, and the numbers it derived. Reading one means checking that the contour sits on the visible edge, that the tip marker is at the tip, and that the printed numbers are consistent with the picture and with one another.

explainers.title: A fluctuation chart is a video turned into numbers: read the picture, then the trace it produced
explainers.summary: Each point on a height or width trace is one video frame reduced to one number. The sampled frames in these figures let you check that the number follows the picture; the seismograph strips show the same traces being drawn as the flame moves.

explainers.title: A decomposition splits a record into parts: read what each part is for and what it cannot say
explainers.summary: POD splits a stack of video frames into spatial patterns ranked by energy. DMD splits it into patterns that each have one frequency and one growth rate. EMD and the Hilbert-Huang spectrum split a single time series into oscillations whose frequency may drift. Each method answers a different question, and each has a known way to mislead.

explainers.title: A measured record has three layers: a scale in millimetres, a signal in time, and a regime label on top
explainers.summary: The time series gives height and width against time with colour bands naming the stage of the flame. The kymograph unrolls the whole flame into one time-height image, so that moving structures appear as slanted stripes. The tracking clip shows where the scale comes from: a ruler beside the burner tube.

explainers.title: A zonal instrument view turns one flame video into many small time series, one per height band
explainers.summary: The tracked flame edge is cut into horizontal height zones, and the flame width in each zone becomes its own trace. Reading the instrument frames tells you what is measured and when; reading the campaign summaries (RMS and coefficient of variation per zone) tells you where along the flame the fluctuation lives and how repeatable that is across runs.

explainers.title: An ensemble figure asks one question: what is common to repeat runs, and how large is the run-to-run spread around it?
explainers.summary: Eight repeat flame runs are aligned at ignition and then compared by frame, by time series, by distribution, by spectrum and by onset time. Reading any of these figures means separating what repeats from run to run (the central curve) from what does not (the spread), and asking which kind of spread each band draws.

explainers.title: A stabilization time is a fitted number with an error bar, and the bars matter as much as the dots
explainers.summary: A burning pool approaches steady burning gradually. The time to reach 90 percent of the steady rate is a single-number summary of that rise. Eight runs give eight such numbers with intervals, and an ignition-aligned median curve shows the shape they summarise.

explainers.title: When several edge finders disagree on the same frame, the disagreement is the measurement uncertainty
explainers.summary: Each segmentation method draws a different outline around the same flame because 'where the edge is' depends on a rule. Overlaying all of them on one real frame shows which rules agree, which depend on the glow, and which fail.

explainers.title: A peaked curve is a mechanism question: why hydrogen and efficiency rise and then fall with steam
explainers.summary: Hydrogen yield, cold-gas efficiency and combustion-zone temperature are all plotted against the same steam-to-fuel ratio, with and without a catalyst. Read them as one story: they peak at the same ratio, which points to temperature as the thing that changes, and not steam alone.

explainers.title: Three audit figures: does the mass add up, what was actually run, and where does the equilibrium baseline fail?
explainers.summary: A Sankey ledger, a design-of-experiments map and a four-panel parity plot are the rigour figures of an experimental campaign. They do not show a result; they show whether the results can be trusted, what they cover, and which simple model is not enough.

explainers.title: A lab photograph is evidence of existence, not of a result: what the flame, the balance and the chromatograph can and cannot show
explainers.summary: Three photographs from the experimental campaign: a producer-gas flame, a laboratory balance and a gas chromatograph. Each stands for one link in the measurement chain (what the rig made, how fuel and samples were weighed, how the gas was analysed). Read them for what they document, and for what the numbers that come from them need in addition.

explainers.title: A feature check builds one operation on a simple shape, so the right answer is known before you look
explainers.summary: Each small plot applies one modelling operation (fillet, circular pattern, revolve, shell, circular sweep) to a simple primitive whose correct result can be stated in a sentence, for example revolve of a rectangle is an annulus and a circular sweep of a disc is a torus. The check is: does the picture match the sentence in its title?

explainers.title: A Boolean screenshot shows two inputs and one result: read the History tree first, then check what the outside view cannot show
explainers.summary: Each figure shows a History with two input bodies and one Boolean node on top, and a view of the result. Union, intersection and subtraction are min and max of two distance fields; the smooth variants round the crease. The picture alone often cannot separate them, but the mesh counts can.

explainers.title: A feature screenshot is a recipe in the History and a result with counts: read the recipe, then test the result against the volume and topology the recipe must give
explainers.summary: Each figure shows the History of a shape built from profiles or primitives plus one feature node (extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet, chamfer, shell), and the resulting body. Every feature has a closed-form volume or topology rule, so the mesh counts and, in the toolbar run, the printed volume and area can be checked by arithmetic.

explainers.title: A primitive screenshot is one History node, one body and one status line: read the node, the scale bar and the mesh counts
explainers.summary: Each figure is a GeoStudio window with a single signed-distance primitive in the History panel, the meshed body in a 3D view, and a status line giving vertex and face counts. It shows that the primitive was built and meshed; the counts let you test, with one identity, whether the surface is closed.

explainers.title: Profiles and patterns: count the copies with the mesh numbers, because the picture cannot tell overlapping copies from one body
explainers.summary: Profile screenshots show a 2D shape wrapped in a thin extrusion so it can be seen; pattern and repeat screenshots show copies of one body. Whether the copies merge or stay separate depends on spacing against size, and the Euler characteristic of the mesh counts the separate pieces exactly: 2V minus F divided by four.

explainers.title: A transform screenshot is one input body and one map: read the node, then ask what the map does to size, orientation and distance
explainers.summary: Each figure shows an input body in the History and a transform node on top. Translate, rotate and mirror preserve distances; scale, taper and free-form deformation do not, and their effect is measured by the Jacobian of the map. Because the input is often a sphere, a transform can look like a no-op, so the counts and the node name carry the evidence.

explainers.title: A cross-engine geometry test draws the same named shape from three kernels and asks whether they agree
explainers.summary: Each named test shape (box, cone, torus, revolved nozzle, ...) is built once by a Gmsh/OpenCASCADE-style boundary-representation kernel, a PicoGK-compatible voxel kernel and a signed-distance-field kernel, tessellated, and drawn in the same viewer. The figure is a visual agreement check: if the three renderings coincide, the shapes are the same to drawing accuracy. Numbers (volume, bounding box, distance between surfaces) are the next, stronger test.

explainers.title: A dominance plot asks: is one operating condition deciding the objective?
explainers.summary: The top row shows how much each condition contributes to a classical average error; the bottom row shows, per condition, whether tuning made the error fraction of nominal go down or up. Together they ask whether an average is a fair summary or whether one outlying condition is steering it.

explainers.title: A hyperparameter heatmap asks: does the answer depend on the settings, or only on the problem?
explainers.summary: Each cell is one complete optimization run at one pair of settings, coloured by the final mean error. The picture is useful when the colours vary smoothly and the whole map spans little; it is misleading when a narrow range is stretched over the full colour bar or when single stochastic runs are read as structure.

explainers.title: An ignition-delay panel asks: does the tuned mechanism pass through the data where the nominal one does not?
explainers.summary: Each panel plots ignition delay on a log axis against 1000/T for one fixed mixture and pressure. Three things share the axes: the nominal mechanism, the tuned mechanism and the experiments with their error bars. The reading is a comparison of distances to the data, condition by condition.

explainers.title: A landscape with a search path asks: is the optimizer finding the best valley, or just the nearest one?
explainers.summary: The same two-parameter problem is drawn as three surfaces, each defined by a different objective, with the starting point, the true optimum and the path a search took. The comparison is about shape: a single smooth bowl is easy for any optimizer, a surface with many valleys is not, and a smoothed starting surface can lead the search into the right valley before the final objective is applied.

explainers.title: A solver-by-objective grid asks: does the answer depend on the optimizer, the objective, or both?
explainers.summary: Nine small landscapes in a three-by-three grid: three optimizers across the columns, three objectives down the rows, each with the start, the true optimum, the search path and two printed numbers. The grid is read by comparing the distance to the true optimum, not the objective value, because the objective is different in every row.

explainers.title: Integrals, areas and lengths as sums of small pieces: six workspaces, one habit of reading the readout
explainers.summary: Six Math Studio screenshots use the same pattern: split a region into n small pieces, add up one quantity per piece, and print the exact value and the error beside the sum. The pieces differ: grid cells with a Jacobian, spherical wedges, boxes, frustum bands, chords and polar cells.

explainers.title: Strands, skins and legs: constraints that are exact against penalties that stretch
explainers.summary: Math Studio's Deform & Hair and Mechanisms workspaces animate three classical geometry-processing ideas. Follow-the-leader hair keeps segment lengths exactly while a spring model lets them stretch; linear blend skinning collapses a twisted joint where dual quaternion skinning keeps its volume; and a Stewart-Gough platform shows how six legs give six degrees of freedom.

explainers.title: A matrix is where it sends the basis vectors: determinant, morph, rotation angles and singular values
explainers.summary: Four Math Studio views of linear maps. In 2D the columns of a matrix are arrows and the determinant is the signed area of the image of the unit square; in 3D, a rotation parametrized by Euler angles loses a degree of freedom at pitch 90 degrees (gimbal lock), and the singular value decomposition splits any matrix into rotate, stretch, rotate.

explainers.title: One solid, two ways to slice it: washers, shells and a cross-section, each with its error printed
explainers.summary: The Revolve workspace builds a solid from a region and shows its volume as a sum of thin pieces. The same solid with a hole is cut into washers (perpendicular to the axis) and into cylindrical shells (parallel to it); a Manim render shows the limit; a Steinmetz solid shows what a clever cross-section can do.

explainers.title: The Solver and the Atlas: finding a formula, crossing a stability limit, reading a phase plane and a saddle
explainers.summary: Four screenshots of the Solver and Atlas workspaces: symbolic regression picks a formula from a Pareto front of complexity against loss; the heat equation is run just beyond its stability limit; the phase plane of a harmonic oscillator shows a centre; and a saddle surface is shown in 2D contours and in 3D.

explainers.title: A benchmark check asks whether each result lies inside a published interval and how it moves with the mesh; a manufactured-solution check asks whether the error falls at the designed rate
explainers.summary: Three panels compare drag, lift and pressure drop for flow past a cylinder in a channel with published reference intervals at two mesh sizes, and two log-log panels give the error of a manufactured three-dimensional Stokes solution at three mesh sizes with measured orders. Read both for what the points can and cannot establish with so few meshes.

explainers.title: Secondary flow and particle focusing are read as trends against Dean number and radius, and a search that finds nothing is evidence only if the search was adequate
explainers.summary: One figure compares secondary-flow strength with two literature scalings across a Dean-number sweep, one records a feature the model did not produce, and one follows particles that migrate across streamlines in a pipe. Read each for its reference, its marked non-converged points, and what the footnote claims beyond the plotted data.

explainers.title: An exact solution tests the solver; a penalization parameter sweep tests how fast an approximate model approaches a reference, and the best setting may not be the largest
explainers.summary: Three checks of the same low-Reynolds-number solver: a pipe profile against the exact parabola, a channel with a Brinkman friction term against its closed-form solution for four friction values, and a Brinkman-penalised solid against a mesh that follows the body. Read each for what it is compared against and which error is controlled by which knob.

explainers.title: Before optimising, check the objective against an energy identity and its gradient against finite differences, and plot the error, not just the two values
explainers.summary: A bar chart compares two ways of computing the power dissipated in a channel flow, and a pair of panels compares an analytic design gradient with central finite differences at two step sizes. Both are pre-optimisation gates: their purpose is to show a small number, so the figure must make small numbers visible.

explainers.title: A channel flow is checked by what must be conserved or known in closed form: the same flux through every arm, and a parabola raised by a wall-slip term
explainers.summary: A colour map of speed in a stepped microchannel and a profile plot of slip flow against no-slip flow at a Knudsen number of 0.05. The first is read through mass conservation and the no-slip wall, the second through the closed-form slip-flow profile and its mean-velocity enhancement.

explainers.title: Each transport demo is checked against a closed form or a balance: a Gaussian pulse for dispersion, an energy balance for heat transfer, and the Boltzmann law for ions near a charged wall
explainers.summary: Three single-physics demonstrations in micro-scale geometry: a solute pulse carried and spread along a channel, temperature in a heated channel wall and fluid, and the electric potential and ion concentrations next to a charged surface. Read each for the law it must obey, the numbers it prints, and whether the printed numbers are consistent with each other.

explainers.title: A condition map shows where a model was trained against where it is asked to work, and colour adds a third quantity to the grid
explainers.summary: Two 3D point clouds fill the same temperature, pressure and equivalence-ratio box. One marks which conditions ignite within a time bound, the other how stiff the chemistry is. A small cluster of circles marks the conditions a reference model was trained on: the maps show how little of the box that is.

explainers.title: A flame-speed bell and an extinction line both measure how fast chemistry can keep up with transport
explainers.summary: The flame-speed figure plots laminar burning velocity against equivalence ratio, one panel per diluent; the extinction figure plots the strain rate at which a counterflow flame goes out. Both are model outputs for the same hydrogen mechanism, and both are controlled by the ratio of reaction rate to diffusion.

explainers.title: A tool screenshot is evidence of a configuration, not of a result: read the inputs, the status and the empty result pane
explainers.summary: Two posters show a desktop tool at the start of a run: a nominal simulation against ignition-delay targets and an ignition-delay sensitivity calculation. The frames show the inputs and a running status. What the inputs mean, and what the finished run is for, is standard combustion-kinetics practice.

explainers.title: An ignition-delay grid is read as lines on a 1000/T plot, and a stirred-reactor curve as a response that jumps once the reactor ignites
explainers.summary: The ignition-delay figure shows time to ignition against inverse temperature in three pressure panels; the reactor figure shows the steady water mole fraction of a stirred reactor against temperature. Both are model outputs, so the reading is about shape, slope and gaps, not about agreement with data.

explainers.title: Before an optimisation run, show the design space; during it, show the cost; when it fails, show the log
explainers.summary: Three views of one demo optimisation run: where the target conditions sit in temperature, pressure and equivalence ratio, the running tool with an empty cost pane, and the log of the failure that stopped it. The reading skills are standard: coverage of a design space, what a progress panel must show, and how to read a traceback.

explainers.title: A rate-of-progress panel ranks the reactions that matter at one condition, and a species trace shows when they take over
explainers.summary: The 3 by 3 grid ranks the eight largest net reaction rates at nine conditions, each panel scaled to its own maximum. The species trace shows one ignition in time: slow growth of intermediates, then a step. Together they show which steps drive the chemistry and when.

explainers.title: A dominance plot asks: is one operating condition deciding the objective?
explainers.summary: The top row shows how much each condition contributes to a classical average error; the bottom row shows, per condition, whether tuning made the error fraction of nominal go down or up. Together they ask whether an average is a fair summary or whether one outlying condition is steering it.

explainers.title: A containment figure asks: does the smaller uncertainty region sit inside the larger one, and when do they coincide?
explainers.summary: Two ellipses in the plane of two retained parameters: the marginal region (the full uncertainty after ignoring a third parameter) and the conditional region (the uncertainty when that third parameter is fixed). When the removed parameter is correlated with the retained ones, the conditional ellipse is strictly inside; when it is not, they are identical.

explainers.title: A hyperparameter heatmap asks: does the answer depend on the settings, or only on the problem?
explainers.summary: Each cell is one complete optimization run at one pair of settings, coloured by the final mean error. The picture is useful when the colours vary smoothly and the whole map spans little; it is misleading when a narrow range is stretched over the full colour bar or when single stochastic runs are read as structure.

explainers.title: An ignition-delay panel asks: does the tuned mechanism pass through the data where the nominal one does not?
explainers.summary: Each panel plots ignition delay on a log axis against 1000/T for one fixed mixture and pressure. Three things share the axes: the nominal mechanism, the tuned mechanism and the experiments with their error bars. The reading is a comparison of distances to the data, condition by condition.

explainers.title: A parity plot asks: does the cheap surrogate reproduce the expensive simulation on points it has not seen?
explainers.summary: Each point pairs the surrogate's estimate with the direct simulation of the same parameter set. Points on the diagonal agree. Training and testing points are drawn differently, and the legend states the largest percentage miss for each, so the picture checks both the fit and its generalization.

explainers.title: A stage-by-stage fit comparison asks: which stage or solver actually moved the model toward the data?
explainers.summary: Several ignition-delay curves are overlaid: the nominal mechanism, the result after each optimization stage, and sometimes the result from different solvers. The legends carry an error number for each curve. The figure is read by checking, condition by condition, whether the printed number and the visible distance to the data agree and whether each stage helped.

explainers.title: A toy landscape and a solver grid ask: does the search find the best valley or only the nearest one?
explainers.summary: The same two-parameter problem is drawn as three surfaces, each defined by a different objective, with the starting point, the true optimum and the path a search took. The comparison is about shape: a single smooth bowl is easy for any optimizer, a surface with many valleys is not, and a smoothed starting surface can lead the search into the right valley before the final objective is applied.

explainers.title: A correlation heatmap shows which parameters move together, and the blocks of red are the ones that cannot be treated independently
explainers.summary: Each heatmap is a symmetric table of Pearson correlations between reactions' parameters across all targets, one per Arrhenius parameter. Read the blocks, not the cells: a block of strongly positive cells means those reactions act as one group.

explainers.title: A confidence ellipse is a level set of the covariance, and dropping a parameter changes its size in a predictable direction
explainers.summary: Three figures show a joint uncertainty ellipsoid reduced to two parameters in two different ways: its shadow (marginal) and its slice (conditional). The conditional ellipse always sits inside the marginal one, and sampling from the wrong matrix factor draws a cloud of the wrong size.

explainers.title: A log-scale bar chart of cost is read as ratios, so the right question is how many times slower, not how many seconds
explainers.summary: The top row shows two sampled curves per method; the bottom bars compare the measured wall-clock time to draw 100 samples on a logarithmic axis. Equal distances on that axis are equal ratios, and the printed times give a slowest-to-fastest ratio of about 11,000, about four decades.

explainers.title: A parity plot asks whether predictions fall on the diagonal, and the test points, not the training points, answer it
explainers.summary: A parity plot puts prediction against truth. Training points on the diagonal only show that the model can reproduce what it was given. Here the training points lie exactly on the line while the held-out test points form a flat cloud, and a small percentage error is partly an artefact of how narrow the response range is.

explainers.title: Sampled rate curves are read against their uncertainty band, and the fit-quality panel says how well each sample respects it
explainers.summary: Each poster shows sampled temperature-dependent rate deviations drawn against 1/T inside a shaded uncertainty band, next to a log-scale objective per sample. The four posters differ in the method that produced the samples; the way to read them is the same: how many curves stay inside the band, what shapes they take, and how the objective behaves.

explainers.title: What a flow cannot do, and how one extra dimension fixes it
explainers.summary: Flows of ODEs cannot cross, so a Neural ODE on the line cannot represent x to minus x, and a planar one cannot unlink two nested rings. Adding one augmented coordinate lets the trajectories pass around each other. These figures show the obstruction, the exact lifted flows that avoid it, and what learned models do.

explainers.title: Wavelets, whitening, activations and an audit: transforms you choose or learn, and the checks they need
explainers.summary: These course animations cover transforms that depend on data or are learned: a sparse wavelet approximation, whitening by PCA, one network layer deforming a grid, and an audit that re-derives the equation a transformed variable must obey. Companion static figures show a wavelet scale map, the three stages of whitening, six activation functions with their derivatives, and two coordinate transforms with their field derivatives.

explainers.title: Depth, initial gain, optimizers and residual blocks: four faces of one differential equation
explainers.summary: Gradient flow through a deep network is a product of layer factors; gradient descent is forward Euler on a gradient flow; momentum is a damped second-order ODE; and a stack of residual blocks is a numerical integrator in depth. These figures show each of these statements at work.

explainers.title: Explicit solvers: accuracy comes from the order, survival from the step size
explainers.summary: Forward Euler and Runge-Kutta methods are drawn as polygons, slope arrows and error surfaces. Two questions are answered by eye: how fast does the error fall as the step shrinks (order), and for which step size does the numerical solution blow up (stability)? Companion static figures add Euler polygons, the energy growth of Euler on the oscillator, measured orders of six methods and a work-precision comparison.

explainers.title: Four routes to one gradient number, and why the one that re-integrates the state backwards can fail
explainers.summary: Training a Neural ODE needs the derivative of a loss through an ODE solve. These figures show the forward pass with its solver steps, the adjoint equation integrated backward on the Van der Pol oscillator, four ways of computing the same number, the instability of re-integrating the state in reverse time, and the commuting diagram that explains when discretize-then-optimize and optimize-then-discretize agree.

explainers.title: Stability regions decide which method can take large steps; implicit methods buy that with a Newton solve
explainers.summary: A stability region is the set of values of h times lambda for which a method's numerical solution decays. These figures draw it as a region, a surface and a plot against step size, and then show what an implicit method does with the freedom: far fewer steps on a stiff problem, at the price of solving an equation each step. Companion static figures add explicit stability regions with real-axis limits, the ROBER stability ceiling, BDF regions, L-stability ringing, a step-size controller and cost against tolerance.

explainers.title: Linear, Mobius, polynomial, Fourier and Laplace maps: each has one failure that the figure is built to show
explainers.summary: These course animations take a classical transformation and put its characteristic failure on screen: transient growth hidden by eigenvalues, circles-to-circles of a Mobius map, Runge's blow-up of equispaced polynomials, aliasing of a fast sinusoid, and the pole positions that decide a decaying response. Companion static figures show a nilpotent shear flow, Mobius classes, a Runge comparison, a 21 and 11 Hz alias, and the resolvent gain of a non-normal matrix.

explainers.title: Charts that tame large rates, and what they cost: a log coordinate, its dead zone, and a power chart
explainers.summary: Replacing a state by its logarithm or a power of it changes the vector field the solver and the optimizer see. These figures show the standard facts about such charts: relative rates replace absolute ones, a clamp creates a zero-gradient dead zone, a power chart compresses eigenvalues but amplifies errors on the way back, and the spectral radius of the transformed field is bounded below by the largest relative rate.

explainers.title: A transformation is judged by what it keeps: orientation, composition and linking
explainers.summary: The first three course animations ask what a map does to space. A map can fold a grid (the Jacobian determinant changes sign), a flow of an ODE composes like a clock (the semigroup law), and some quantities, such as a linking number, survive any smooth deformation without tearing. Companion static figures show the determinant of a squaring map, a two-to-one fold, trajectories that cannot cross, and linked rings under a flow.

explainers.title: Scaling the variables changes the loss geometry, not the dynamics: conditioning explains why one optimizer needs one step and another 60000
explainers.summary: A diagonal rescaling of the state leaves an ODE's eigenvalues unchanged but reweights the squared-error loss, which changes the curvature of the loss surface by a factor that can reach millions. These figures show the effect on the vector field, on a Runge-Kutta solver, on the loss surface and on how many iterations gradient descent and Adam need.

explainers.title: Reading a vector field: existence by iteration, fixed points by eigenvalues, and what a truncation costs
explainers.summary: These figures introduce an ODE as a field of arrows. Picard iteration builds the solution, the trace-determinant plane sorts fixed points into eight portraits, and error curves show how a crude method or a truncated linear lift fails. Companion static figures show the oscillator phase portrait, Gronwall bounds for three systems, the full trace-determinant plane and phase portraits of classic systems.

explainers.title: A transform is only as good as its inverse: reading the cost of power, log, quantile, tanh and polar maps
explainers.summary: Each of these course animations applies a one-line transform to data or to a grid and then prints what it costs: error amplification of a power map, the plateau of a log scale, a heavy tail against normal quantiles, round-off at the saturated end of tanh, the jump of an angle chart, the local stretch of a conformal map. Companion static figures add the slope of the power map at the origin, a clamp against an additive epsilon, the Box-Cox slope, float64 round-trip errors, a branch cut, and four curvilinear grids.

explainers.title: Stiffness has a geometry: a slow curve inside a fast-contracting sheet, drawn two ways
explainers.summary: These figures use the classic ROBER test problem to show what stiffness looks like: a trajectory that hugs a slow manifold, a step size set by the fast clock and not by the accuracy needed, a conservation law that can be kept exactly or only approximately, and a resolvent surface that shows the eigenvalues. Companion static figures add the eigenvector-conditioning surface along the ROBER orbit and the RK45 against BDF step counts and step-size traces.

explainers.title: A bar chart of arms is a claim about a difference: check the baseline, the spread and the scale before believing it
explainers.summary: Three Playground figures compare arms of an experiment with bars: normalization arms against a raw baseline, a linear against a nonlinear model on two toy datasets, and three weight-decay settings. Each answers 'which arm is better?', and each is easy to over-read.

explainers.title: Where the test points sit decides what a test score can promise
explainers.summary: A split figure shows the parameter space of a simulated data set and colours each case train, validation or test. If every test case is surrounded by training cases, a good score certifies interpolation only. These figures also show what the corresponding trajectories look like in each split and a design that adds true extrapolation points.

explainers.title: Inside the network: gradient size by layer, input features as filters, and what the last layer does to the classes
explainers.summary: These Playground figures look inside a model instead of at its score: how large the gradient is in each parameter during training, how depth changes the gradient reaching the first layer, what each input feature looks like as a picture, and how the final-layer embedding separates two classes.

explainers.title: Reading a reinforcement-learning optimizer: where it walks, what it earns, and what it may claim
explainers.summary: Eight Playground figures follow an agent that tunes model weights by reinforcement learning: its path through a 2D slice of weight space, the objective and reward over training, the size of its actions, the autocorrelation of its reward, and a matched-budget comparison with two classical optimizers that ends in a verdict. Each tells you something different about whether the agent is learning or wandering.

explainers.title: A training curve is a diary: read the slope, the spikes and the gap, not just the last value
explainers.summary: Four Playground figures draw loss or accuracy against epoch: an eleven-optimizer race on a small Van der Pol benchmark, a train-versus-validation tour, a linear readout against a decoder head, and an initialization failure. The same habits apply to each: log axis, same budget, look for plateaus and spikes.

explainers.title: A bar of 'number of reactions per case' asks how large each surrogate-model problem is
explainers.summary: For every ignition-delay target the sensitivity threshold keeps a different number of reactions. The bar chart counts them: high-temperature cases sit in one band, low-temperature cases in another, and one case can stand out. The count controls how many simulations a quadratic surrogate needs.

explainers.title: A curve-sample figure asks what shapes a rate coefficient can take while staying inside its stated uncertainty
explainers.summary: A rate coefficient is a line on an Arrhenius plot. Its uncertainty is a band around that line. Three Arrhenius parameters can vary, so the samples inside the band can be parallel shifts, tilts about a pivot, or curved arches. The figures show which of these a sampling rule produces and whether samples respect the limits.

explainers.title: A bootstrap band asks how much the fitted curve could move if the measurements had been slightly different
explainers.summary: Eight measured ignition delays are joined by an interpolating curve. To show how uncertain that curve is, the data are perturbed by a small random jitter many times and re-interpolated. The band is where 95 percent of those re-interpolated curves lie. It is wide where the curve has little support and narrow where points constrain it.

explainers.title: A sensitivity bar chart asks which few reactions control the answer, and whether that list changes with temperature
explainers.summary: Each bar is how strongly the ignition delay responds to a small change in one reaction's rate. Long bars are the reactions worth tuning, bars inside the dashed 5 percent lines are dropped, and comparing two temperatures shows that the controlling reactions are different in different regimes.

explainers.title: An ignition-delay comparison asks one question: does the tuned mechanism sit closer to the measurements than the nominal one, everywhere that matters?
explainers.summary: Ignition delay is plotted on a log axis against 1000/T, where a single Arrhenius-controlled process is a straight line. Measured points with error bars are compared with two simulated lines, nominal and optimized. A better mechanism is one whose line passes through more error bars, without moving a good region to fix a bad one.

explainers.title: An uncertainty-versus-temperature plot asks whether a smooth curve can honour the few values an expert reported
explainers.summary: A rate coefficient's uncertainty factor is reported at a handful of temperatures. A smooth function of temperature is needed everywhere in between. The plot overlays the reported values (dots) with a smooth construction (green) and a literature version (red), and shows where they agree and where a smooth form cannot follow the data.

explainers.title: A parity plot asks whether the surrogate reproduces the simulation, and whether it still does where the search goes
explainers.summary: Each dot is one parameter set: the simulation value on x, the surrogate prediction on y. If the surrogate were perfect every dot would sit on the diagonal. The figures show that for training, testing and search points the dots hug the line, and that the numbers in the legend, not the picture, tell the size of the worst miss.

explainers.title: A per-case error scatter asks which targets the surrogate model can be trusted for, and whether it is as good where the search goes as on fresh points
explainers.summary: Each dot is one target. The log y axis shows the worst relative error of the surrogate against the full simulation, for two kinds of points. Most cases sit near or below 1 percent, a few are far worse, and the testing set is usually worse than the points the search actually visited.

explainers.title: A variance inflation factor says how well one input can be rebuilt from the others, and two red bars here say two inputs are nearly the same
explainers.summary: The left panel is a correlation matrix of the candidate inputs and the target; the right panel converts the same information into one number per input, the variance inflation factor (VIF). Two inputs sit far beyond the usual threshold of 10, so the check does not confirm that the inputs are non-redundant.

explainers.title: From one curve to the ingredients: why restricted Hartree-Fock fails at dissociation, what an orbital looks like, and what J and K are
explainers.summary: Three course figures cover the basic vocabulary of electronic structure. The H2 energy curve compares methods against the exact (full CI) answer in a minimal setting; polar plots show the angular shape of s and p orbitals; two small matrices list the Coulomb and exchange integrals that enter every Hartree-Fock energy.

explainers.title: Reading a basis-set heat map and a conformer: what the overlap matrix and a projected geometry can and cannot tell
explainers.summary: A heat map of orbital overlaps shows how atomic orbitals of a molecule talk to each other in a minimal basis, and a pair of projections shows a sampled molecular conformer. Both are inputs to quantum chemistry, not results, and both come with caveats stated in their titles.

explainers.title: A potential energy surface turns into a rate: saddle, path, barrier, and the exponential that connects them to temperature
explainers.summary: The hydrogen exchange reaction H + H2 is the textbook case. A contour map gives the surface, a profile along the minimum-energy path gives the barrier, and an Eyring plot shows how a barrier of a given height becomes a rate at each temperature. Two further figures draw the same reaction on a LEPS model surface.

explainers.title: Looking inside: a projection of the learned states, and a grid of layers that saturate or do not
explainers.summary: Two SciML diagnostics of a learned model's inner workings. A principal-component plot shows the states it visits as a thin, almost one-dimensional sheet; a grid of small panels shows, for each architecture variant, how much of the first layer is saturated and how large the activation slope is.

explainers.title: A learned ODE can be too stiff to integrate and too wrong to time an ignition: diagnostics to plot beside the loss
explainers.summary: Five SciML figures look at a learned model of ignition from the outside: how stiff its own Jacobian becomes during training, how its predicted ignition delay compares with the reference, a timing proxy against initial temperature, and the first attempt whose smooth loss curve hid a failed prediction.

explainers.title: Before ranking runs, draw the noise: seed bands, bootstrap intervals and the error floor behind a percent error
explainers.summary: Two SciML figures ask whether differences between many training runs are real. One ranks all runs with confidence intervals and a seed-noise band; the other plots percent error against the size of the true value on log-log axes, where a fixed absolute error appears as a line of slope minus one.

explainers.title: Small multiples of prediction against reference: one panel per variable, plus the curves and drifts that back them up
explainers.summary: These SciML figures check a surrogate of an ignition problem the way an engineer would: a training and validation curve pair, a grid with one panel per species and temperature at a fixed condition, a replication grid at four conditions, and the drift of conserved elements.

explainers.title: A turbulence spectrum asks where the energy sits in scale, and whether a model keeps it there
explainers.summary: Spectra, structure functions, correlations and increment PDFs are five views of the same question: how is fluctuation energy shared between large and small scales? Each one is read against a reference (a slope, a Gaussian, a zero line) and each has a regime in which the reference does not apply.

explainers.title: Vortex identification asks whether the local flow rotates or strains, and where the threshold is drawn
explainers.summary: Vorticity alone cannot tell a vortex from a shear layer. The Okubo-Weiss parameter and the Q-criterion compare rotation with strain point by point; the Q-R diagram and the quadrant plot compress the same kind of information into statistics, at the price of losing position.

explainers.title: A force coefficient is a number with a window, a domain and a reference; read all three before the value
explainers.summary: Drag and lift coefficients on a cylinder are the standard check of a flow solver. The figures here show how to read a force time series, a steady drag plateau, a resolution study and a blockage comparison, and why each can disagree with a published value for reasons other than the solver being wrong.

explainers.title: A vortex street is read as a sign pattern: thin attached layers, then alternating eddies at a fixed spacing
explainers.summary: The vorticity map of flow past a cylinder shows two thin layers of opposite sign on the body and a row of alternating eddies downstream. Reading it means checking the colour scale, the sign of each layer, the eddy spacing and the time at which the map was taken.

explainers.title: Validating a turbulence closure means plotting wall-unit profiles against DNS, and saying what the numbers can and cannot show
explainers.summary: Closure-versus-DNS figures all use wall units: mean velocity against distance from the wall on a log axis, with the viscous sublayer and log law as reference. The same few checks apply whether the figure shows a mean profile, an eddy-viscosity profile, a fitted coefficient, an error scorecard or a colour-coded anisotropy state.

explainers.title: A budget figure asks which terms balance, by how much, and whether the balance actually closes
explainers.summary: Budget plots lay every term of a transport equation on one axis so that the dominant balance can be seen and the residual checked. The same reading applies to the turbulent-kinetic-energy budget of a channel and to the term-by-term view of an iterative solver's own convergence.

explainers.title: A vorticity map is only honest on a fixed, symmetric colour scale, and it needs a number beside it
explainers.summary: Colour maps of vorticity, filtered fields, difference fields and their videos show where the structures are. They cannot say how much energy they hold or how fast it decays, so every such figure must be read with its colour limits and paired with a spectrum or a time history.

explainers.title: A design sweep is a map of a trade-off: read the axis range before the shape
explainers.summary: A one-parameter sweep (pressure drop against bore) and a two-parameter heatmap (required length against bore and wall superheat) are the two basic ways to size equipment. Both are only as informative as their axis ranges: a curve that looks steep can span a few percent, and a heatmap that looks complicated can depend on one variable.

explainers.title: Reading a staged heating profile: fluid core, wall and ceiling along the tube, then across the wall
explainers.summary: Axial temperature profiles show what the fluid and the wall are doing stage by stage along a heated tube; the radial profile shows where the temperature drop sits across the wall and the fluid film. Together they answer one question: does the wall stay under its ceiling while the fluid goes from liquid to superheated vapour?

explainers.title: Two clocks, one step size: why stiffness limits the solver and why a change of coordinates must be checked
explainers.summary: A pair of exponentials with time scales 1 and 0.01 sets the stage; an explicit solver with the wrong step then blows up; and the rest of the group asks what survives a change of variables: eigenvalues, a log transform with a floor, and a progress variable that is not a clock.

explainers.title: A complete small learning loop: fit with Adam, test beyond the training window, and check the gradient three ways
explainers.summary: A toy decay problem carries the whole workflow: a training curve, a rollout from an unseen start beyond the training time, a forward-and-backward diagram, and four ways of computing one gradient that all agree to nine digits.

explainers.title: Making nonlinear dynamics look linear: lifts, snapshot fits and low-dimensional models
explainers.summary: Koopman lifting, dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and latent Neural ODEs share one idea: find coordinates in which a linear or low-dimensional description is enough, and then check that it is.

explainers.title: Which channel is loud? Scaling, gradients, power means and a loss landscape as four views of the same question
explainers.summary: Four toy charts of what a loss function emphasizes. Raw squared residuals let one loud channel drown a quiet one; a loud loss is not the same as a loud gradient; a power mean turns the same errors into different aggregates; and an optimizer on a stretched landscape zigzags.

explainers.title: Round it, export it, compare it: the checks that remain after the model is trained
explainers.summary: The last Playground slides turn from training to use: rounding weights to a grid, exporting a rate network without its solver, changing one layer at a time, and keeping the comparison honest. The chart gives one concrete test: roll the whole trajectory out again after the change.

explainers.title: State, rate, trajectory: the three things a Neural ODE must not confuse
explainers.summary: The opening slides of the Playground mini-course are small block diagrams. Read together they say one thing: a Neural ODE does not predict the next state, it learns a rate, and a separate solver turns the rate into a trajectory.

explainers.title: Put the structure in the model: valid inertia, valid rates, graphs, and what a sensor can see
explainers.summary: A robot arm makes state and rate concrete, and four diagram slides say what a model can be forced to respect: a positive-definite mass matrix, domain constraints for mechanics and chemistry, a graph of who interacts, and a sensor map that hides part of the state.

explainers.title: A curve family over a parameter: how does the curve move as the knob turns?
explainers.summary: Several curves of the same formula drawn on one pair of axes, one per value of a parameter. You see what the parameter does to the whole shape, not only to one number.

explainers.title: A function and its derivative on one shared axis: where is it steep, flat or singular?
explainers.summary: Two stacked panels with the same x axis: the function above, its derivative below. Zeros of the derivative line up with the flat spots of the function, and numerical check dots show the derivative was verified.

explainers.title: A parametric and a polar curve: what path does it trace, and which way?
explainers.summary: A curve given by x(t), y(t) or by r(theta) is drawn as a path in the plane. Equal axis scales keep shapes honest and colour along the path tells you the direction of travel.

explainers.title: A piecewise or kink curve: where does it switch regime?
explainers.summary: A curve built from different rules on different intervals. Shaded bands name each regime and marked breakpoints show exactly where the rule changes, so a corner is read as a change of law and not as a plotting glitch.

explainers.title: An envelope and decay with time constants: how fast does it relax?
explainers.summary: A ringing signal drawn inside its decaying envelope, with markers at one, two and three time constants. The time constant tau turns 'how fast' into a number you can read off the axis.

explainers.title: Log, semi-log, log-log and symlog views: does it follow a power or exponential law?
explainers.summary: The same data drawn on four axis types. A straight line on semi-log means an exponential law, a straight line on log-log means a power law, and symlog keeps zero and negative values visible.

explainers.title: An implicit curve and level set: where is f(x, y) = c?
explainers.summary: Contour lines of a function of two variables, each labelled with its value. Where the level changes character (a critical level) the topology of the curve changes, and the plot highlights that level.

explainers.title: A dimensionless universal curve collapse: do different cases fall on one curve?
explainers.summary: Data from several cases look different in raw units. Rescaled by the right combination of the case parameter they fall on one master curve, which shows the physics depends only on that combination.

explainers.title: Contour and slice field: what does the field look like?
explainers.summary: A filled-contour map of a scalar on a plane, with a colour bar, a few contour lines and a marked slice. It is the first picture of any simulation: where the flow is fast, where it spreads and where the structure lives.

explainers.title: Wall-resolution map (y+): is the near-wall mesh right for the model?
explainers.summary: A colour map of y+ on a wall surface and a line of its span average against streamwise position, with the target band shaded. It checks that the first cell sits where the wall model expects it.

explainers.title: Profile lines against reference data: does it match experiment or DNS?
explainers.summary: Mean velocity profile in wall units on a log axis, with two model curves and the reference as open markers, and a small inset of the deviation. The standard check of a turbulence model against DNS or experiment.

explainers.title: Energy spectrum with slope reference: is there an inertial range?
explainers.summary: Turbulent kinetic energy per wavenumber on log-log axes with a k to the minus five thirds line for comparison. A straight stretch parallel to the reference is the inertial range; the roll-off at high k is dissipation or grid resolution.

explainers.title: Anisotropy invariant map (Lumley triangle)
explainers.summary: A plot of the second and third invariants of the Reynolds-stress anisotropy tensor inside a curvilinear triangle. Each point is a state of the turbulence: isotropic at the bottom corner, one-component at the top, two-component along the curved edge.

explainers.title: Vortex identification (Q and lambda2 iso-surfaces): where are the coherent structures?
explainers.summary: A three-dimensional view of the region where a vortex criterion exceeds a threshold, so the tube-like structures of a turbulent flow stand out from the background. The threshold decides what you see.

explainers.title: Budget bars (production, dissipation, transport): what balances what?
explainers.summary: A bar chart of the terms of a transport equation, positive for sources and negative for sinks, with the leftover residual drawn as its own bar. It tests whether the budget of turbulent kinetic energy closes.

explainers.title: Mesh and geometry views: is the grid adequate?
explainers.summary: A picture of the whole computational mesh and a zoom at the wall that shows the first-cell height and the growth of the cells. It lets you judge resolution where the flow changes fastest.

explainers.title: Verification: grid convergence and manufactured solutions
explainers.summary: Two panels: error against grid spacing on log-log axes with the observed order, and a quantity of interest against grid spacing with a Richardson extrapolation and a grid-convergence-index band. It asks whether the solver solves its equations at the expected rate.

explainers.title: Residual history and monitor points: has the run converged?
explainers.summary: Normalised residuals against iteration on a log axis, with a tolerance line, above a monitor signal from the flow. Falling residuals are necessary; a flat monitor is the evidence that the answer has stopped changing.

explainers.title: Detection overlay on a real frame: is the detection right?
