explainers.summary: A contour found by an algorithm drawn over the original image, with a scale bar. It lets you judge by eye whether the detected edge sits where the object's edge is.

explainers.title: Calibration overlay and ruler: is the pixel scale right?
explainers.summary: An image with a feature of known size marked by two picked points, the resulting millimetres per pixel, and a scale bar. It checks the conversion from pixels to physical units before any measurement is trusted.

explainers.title: Time series of tip, width and fluctuation: how does the flame fluctuate?
explainers.summary: Three stacked traces sharing one time axis: a height, a width and the height's deviation from its mean, with the sampling rate stated. It shows rhythm, amplitude and whether the signals move together.

explainers.title: Zonal and ensemble statistics: how does it vary across zones and runs?
explainers.summary: Box plots of a measured quantity by zone along the flame, with the sample count under each zone and the zone mean of each repeat run drawn on top. It shows the trend along the flame, the spread within a zone and the repeatability between runs.

explainers.title: Process schematic and P&ID: how is the rig built?
explainers.summary: A flow diagram of a rig with boxes for equipment, arrows for flow, a symbol for a valve and numbered circles for instruments. It shows what is connected to what, in which direction things flow and where the measurements are taken.

explainers.title: Spectrogram or wavelet of a measured signal: what frequencies are present over time?
explainers.summary: A colour map of signal power against time and frequency, above the raw trace. It shows when a tone is present, how its frequency changes and whether harmonics appear.

explainers.title: Measurement-versus-model parity plot
explainers.summary: Every model prediction is plotted against its measurement, with a 1:1 line, a percentage band and error metrics. Points on the line are perfect agreement; the scatter around it is the error.

explainers.title: Architecture and flow diagram: how is the software or method structured?
explainers.summary: Boxes grouped into horizontal layers, joined by arrows that show which part feeds which. It teaches you to read a software or method diagram: what the layers are, what the arrows mean and what is left out.

explainers.title: Curriculum and dependency map: what depends on what?
explainers.summary: A directed acyclic graph of topics, drawn left to right by level, with arrows from prerequisite to dependent and a colour for done, current and upcoming. It tells you what has to be learned first and what is open to learn next.

explainers.title: Table with row and column sums: do the numbers add up?
explainers.summary: A matrix of counts with a row-sum column, a column-sum row and a grand total, plus an explicit check that the totals agree. It teaches the habit of reading margins before cells.

explainers.title: Stacked ledger (bars): where does the total come from?
explainers.summary: Bars divided into stacked parts with a line of markers showing each bar's total. The total is visible, the first part is easy to compare, and the later parts need care.

explainers.title: Timeline of a project or research journey: how did the work evolve?
explainers.summary: A horizontal time line with dated events alternately above and below, coloured by the kind of event. It shows the order of steps, setbacks and outcomes, and invites a check on whether the spacing is proportional to time.

explainers.title: Slider-parameter sweep with live readout: what if I change this?
explainers.summary: A plot that redraws when a slider moves, with the current curve drawn bold, other settings as faint ghosts, a panel of parameters with units and a readout of derived numbers. It teaches you to read an interactive model: what the controls are and what stays fixed.

explainers.title: Linked 2D and 3D views: how do the views correspond?
explainers.summary: A top-down contour view and a 3D surface of the same function, with one shared selected point marked in both and its values quoted. It teaches you to follow a point between representations.

explainers.title: Timeline-scrubbed animation (play, loop, speed): what happens over time?
explainers.summary: A strip of key frames sharing one clock, with a time slider, play, loop and speed controls. It teaches you to read an animation in print: frames are samples of one continuous history, and the slider says which one you are looking at.

explainers.title: Comparison race: which is faster, live?
explainers.summary: Several runs plotted against one clock, a vertical marker at the current time, a leaderboard of progress at that time and a time slider. It teaches you to read a race: what is measured, against what and at which instant.

explainers.title: Decision surface and arena: what would the model do here?
explainers.summary: A colour map of a classifier's probability over feature space, the decision boundary at one half, the training data on top and a cursor that reports the model's answer at one point. It shows the model's behaviour everywhere, not just on the data.

explainers.title: Embedded notebook with live figures: can I read the derivation and run it?
explainers.summary: A mock-up of a notebook page: a short derivation, the code cell that makes the figure, the figure itself and a note on reproducibility. It teaches you to read a notebook as an argument: text, code and output are three parts of one claim.

explainers.title: A region before and after a map: how are areas and shapes changed?
explainers.summary: A coloured region in the (u, v) plane on the left, its image under a map on the right, with the same colouring on both sides. The Jacobian determinant tells you by what factor small areas were scaled and whether orientation was kept.

explainers.title: A deformed grid: where does the coordinate system stretch or fold?
explainers.summary: A regular grid is pushed through a map. The bent grid shows, at a glance, where cells are squeezed, stretched, sheared or folded over. The original grid is kept faint underneath as a reference.

explainers.title: A Jacobian determinant and condition heat map: where is the map singular or ill-conditioned?
explainers.summary: Two heat maps of a map's local behaviour: the determinant, which says how areas scale and where orientation flips, and the condition number, which says how lopsided the local stretch is. Singular places (fold curves) show as amber contours.

explainers.title: A vector field and its flow lines: which way does the flow go?
explainers.summary: Short arrows give the local direction and size of a field at grid points; streamlines show where the flow goes globally. Together they show sources, sinks, circulation and closed orbits.

explainers.title: A cyclic-colormap angle field: how does phase or direction vary?
explainers.summary: A quantity that is an angle, such as the argument of a complex function, wraps around: just after pi comes minus pi. A cyclic colour map makes the colour seam disappear, so singular points show as places where all colours meet.

explainers.title: Chart switching and atlas overlap: where do charts cover and where do they fail?
explainers.summary: A curved space cannot always be labelled by one coordinate system. Several charts, each good on part of the space, cover it together, and a transition map converts between them wherever they overlap.

explainers.title: A metric ellipse field: how does local distance scale vary?
explainers.summary: At each grid point a small ellipse shows the set of unit-length vectors under the local metric. A small ellipse means distance is costly in those directions; a large ellipse means it is cheap. Direction and anisotropy are read from the ellipse axes.

explainers.title: Riemann rectangles and convergence: how does the sum approach the integral?
explainers.summary: Rectangles under a curve approximate its integral. A second panel plots the error against the number of rectangles on log-log axes, where a straight line of slope -p means the error shrinks like n to the power -p.

explainers.title: An integrand with signed shading: what is positive and what is negative area?
explainers.summary: The area between a curve and the axis is shaded teal where the function is positive and rose where it is negative. Net area is the signed sum: equal pieces of opposite sign cancel to zero.

explainers.title: A slice decomposition with A(x): how is the solid built up?
explainers.summary: A solid of revolution is cut into thin disks across its axis. The left panel shows the slices, one of them highlighted; the right panel plots the area A(x) of each slice, and the area under that curve is the volume.

explainers.title: A double-integral region cut two ways: does the order of integration matter?
explainers.summary: The same region is sliced into vertical strips on the left and horizontal strips on the right. Each way gives its own limits of integration; for a well-behaved integrand both orders give the same value.

explainers.title: A solid of revolution with cut-away: what does it look like inside?
explainers.summary: A 3D view of a solid made by spinning a profile about an axis, with a quarter removed so the interior shows. The profile curve, the axis and the cut planes are marked in different colours.

explainers.title: Circles of curvature and osculating frames: how much does the path bend here?
explainers.summary: At chosen points of a curve the best-fitting circle (the osculating circle) is drawn, with its centre and radius, together with the tangent and normal directions. A small circle means a sharp bend; a huge circle means nearly straight.

explainers.title: A Taylor and series approximation fan: how good is the approximation, and where?
explainers.summary: A function drawn with polynomial approximations of increasing order, and a second panel with the error on a log axis. Inside the radius of convergence the error collapses as the order grows; outside it blows up.

explainers.title: The convergence region of a series in the complex plane: where does it converge?
explainers.summary: A series with a complex variable converges in a disk (power series) or an annulus (Laurent series). Colouring the plane by convergence and drawing the boundary circles shows the region and its edges at a glance.

explainers.title: A free-body and force diagram: which forces act?
explainers.summary: The body is drawn alone, with every force on it as an arrow from its point of application. Arrow length is proportional to the force with a stated scale, and colour names the kind of force. The diagram is the first step to Newton's second law.

explainers.title: A mechanism at several positions: what is the motion cycle?
explainers.summary: A linkage drawn in many positions at once. Faint ghosted copies show the sweep, one bold copy is the current position, a dotted curve is the path of a chosen point, and a star marks the instantaneous centre of the coupler.

explainers.title: A trajectory with velocity arrows: where does it go and how fast?
explainers.summary: The path of a body in the plane, with arrows showing its velocity at equal time steps. With and without air drag on one plot, the arrows show how drag shortens the range and steepens the descent.

explainers.title: Stacked kinematics, x, v and a against t: how are position, velocity and acceleration linked?
explainers.summary: Three panels share one time axis: position on top, velocity in the middle, acceleration at the bottom. Each lower panel is the slope of the one above, so features line up vertically and the chain of derivatives can be read by eye.

explainers.title: An energy budget as stacked areas: where does the energy go?
explainers.summary: Kinetic, potential and dissipated energy are stacked in time, so their sum is the total. A dashed line at the starting energy shows where the total should sit. For a damped oscillator, mechanical energy drains steadily into heat.

explainers.title: A friction circle and limit curves: when does it slip?
explainers.summary: Acceleration demands are plotted as points in the plane of lateral against longitudinal acceleration. The limit of available friction is a circle: points inside grip, points outside slip.

explainers.title: A phase portrait with nullclines: what are the equilibria and their stability?
explainers.summary: For a two-variable system the plane of the two variables is filled with flow lines. The nullclines (where one variable stops changing) cross at the equilibria, and the type of each equilibrium (stable spiral, saddle, ...) is read from the flow around it.

explainers.title: A Poincare section and limit cycle: is the motion periodic or chaotic?
explainers.summary: A long trajectory is reduced to the points where it pierces a chosen plane in one direction. A periodic orbit leaves a few repeating points; a chaotic one leaves a scattered set that traces out a thin curve or fractal.

explainers.title: A moving-frame plot: how does it look from the rotating frame?
explainers.summary: The same motion is drawn twice, in a fixed (inertial) frame and in a frame that turns at constant rate. A straight line in the inertial frame becomes a looping curve in the rotating one, which is where the Coriolis and centrifugal effects come from.

explainers.title: Convergence plot with fitted slopes: what is the observed order?
explainers.summary: The standard test that a numerical method converges at its design rate. Error is plotted against step size on log-log axes, so an error that scales as a power of h becomes a straight line whose slope is the observed order.

explainers.title: Absolute-stability region: which h*lambda are stable?
explainers.summary: The picture that tells you, for a given time-stepping method, which values of the scaled eigenvalue h lambda keep the numerical solution bounded. The stability region is a shaded area of the complex plane; the problem's eigenvalues are plotted on top of it.

explainers.title: Eigenvalue scatter with unit circle: are the discrete eigenvalues inside the stable disc?
explainers.summary: The same stability question as F5.2 seen from the other side: instead of scaled eigenvalues in the z-plane, you plot the eigenvalues mu = R(h lambda) of one time step and check whether they lie inside the unit circle.

explainers.title: Step-size trace vs stability ceiling: is the adaptive solver limited by accuracy or stability?
explainers.summary: For stiff problems an adaptive solver's step size is often set by stability, not by accuracy. This trace puts the accepted step h(t) beside a ceiling computed from the fastest eigenvalue, so you can see which of the two is in charge at each moment.

explainers.title: Conservation drift: does it preserve the invariant?
explainers.summary: Many physical systems have a quantity that should stay constant, such as energy. This plot shows how far each method's value strays, on a log axis, with the machine-epsilon floor drawn as a reference.

explainers.title: Error surface over step and method: which method wins where?
explainers.summary: A colour map of the global error as a function of step size (across) and method (down). Stars mark the method with the smallest error at each step size, so the map shows where a higher-order method really pays off.

explainers.title: Condition number versus parameter: where is the problem ill-conditioned?
explainers.summary: The condition number measures how much a problem amplifies input error. Plotted on a log axis against a parameter, it shows where in the parameter range a linear solve or any other computation loses digits.

explainers.title: Aliasing and sampling overlay: what is lost by sampling?
explainers.summary: Sampling a continuous signal at too low a rate makes a high frequency masquerade as a low one. The plot overlays the true signal, the samples and the apparent alias in time, and shows the same fact as a fold about the Nyquist frequency in frequency.

explainers.title: Work-precision diagram: which solver is cheapest for a target accuracy?
explainers.summary: The fair way to compare numerical solvers: plot the cost (function evaluations) against the error actually achieved, on log-log axes. The cheapest solver for a given accuracy is the lowest curve at that error.

explainers.title: Eigenvalue-versus-time (symlog): how stiff is it along the trajectory?
explainers.summary: How stiff is the problem right now? The real part of the fastest eigenvalue is plotted against time on a symmetric-log axis, so very large negative values and values near zero can sit on one scale. Two curves compare coordinate systems.

explainers.title: Latent-space projection coloured by physics: does the latent space organise by physics?
explainers.summary: A learned latent space is only useful if it is organised by something physical. Project it to two dimensions and colour each point by a known physical quantity: if the colour varies smoothly over the picture, the latent space has captured that quantity.

explainers.title: Eigenvalue compression before/after transform: did the transform reduce stiffness?
explainers.summary: A transformation of variables is only worth it if it makes the problem easier. Two bar charts of the eigenvalue magnitudes of the Jacobian, before and after, on the same log axis, with the stiffness ratio printed on each panel.

explainers.title: State-simplex trajectory (3D, coloured by log time): does the orbit stay physical?
explainers.summary: Mole or mass fractions that must add to one live on a triangle. This plot draws a three-species trajectory in the corner-to-corner geometry of the simplex, coloured by logarithmic time, with the exact and the learned orbit overlaid.

explainers.title: Key-frame strip of an animation: what happens over time, at a glance?
explainers.summary: When a result is an animation, a strip of key frames with time stamps shows what happens at a glance, on paper or in a report. Four frames of a moving blob illustrate the form.

explainers.title: Training audit trace (seeds thin, mean bold): is the result real or seed noise?
explainers.summary: A single training run can look like progress that is only luck. This audit trace draws every random seed as a thin line, the mean as a bold line and a noise floor, so you can see whether an improvement is larger than the run-to-run noise.

explainers.title: Dead-fraction and loss-landscape maps: where does training fail?
explainers.summary: Two heat maps over the same grid of hyper-parameters: how many hidden units are dead, and how low the final loss gets. Loss contours are drawn on both, so the good region can be compared with the failure region.

explainers.title: Commutative diagram with mismatch arrow: do two routes give the same answer?
explainers.summary: A commutative diagram asks whether two different routes between the same start and end give the same answer. Here: encode then flow in the latent space versus flow in the true space then encode, with the mismatch written on an arrow.

explainers.title: Adjoint-gradient check (adjoint vs finite difference): is the gradient right?
explainers.summary: Before training with a hand-derived or adjoint gradient, check it against finite differences. Two panels: a parity plot of the two gradients, and the absolute error per parameter on a log axis with the finite-difference noise floor.

explainers.title: Rollout error growth with horizon: how fast does error accumulate in autoregressive use?
explainers.summary: When a model is applied to its own output step after step, small errors feed on themselves. This plot shows the error against the number of steps (the horizon) on a log axis, with an exponential reference line for the growth rate.

explainers.title: Optimizer race (best-so-far vs evaluations): which converges faster at equal budget?
explainers.summary: The standard way to compare optimizers: the best objective value found so far, against the number of function evaluations, for several optimizers, each repeated many times, shown as a median line and a band over the repeats.

explainers.title: Regret and rank plot across test problems: which optimizer is best on average?
explainers.summary: To say which optimizer is best on average, run them on many test problems, rank them on each, and compare the mean ranks. A critical-difference diagram draws the mean ranks on one axis and joins the optimizers that are not significantly different.

explainers.title: Landscape surface with trajectory: where did the search go?
explainers.summary: A surface plot of the objective with the search path drawn on it shows where an optimizer went: how it moved over ridges and valleys, where it started and where it ended. The example is the Rastrigin function, a landscape with many local minima.

explainers.title: Hyper-parameter heatmap per solver: how sensitive is each solver to its settings?
explainers.summary: Every solver has settings. A heat map of success rate over two settings, one panel per solver on a shared colour scale, shows how sensitive each solver is, and whether its good region is wide or a needle.

explainers.title: Pareto front: what are the trade-offs?
explainers.summary: When there are two goals that conflict, there is usually no single best design: there is a front of designs where improving one goal costs the other. The Pareto plot shows all candidates, marks the non-dominated ones, and points out the knee.

explainers.title: Objective comparison on one problem (e.g. classical vs power-mean): does the objective change the answer?
explainers.summary: The objective you minimise changes the answer. The same data are fitted with two objectives (a classical sum of squares and a robust alternative) under the same budget, and the fits and their errors are shown together.

explainers.title: Ablation dot plot: which component matters?
explainers.summary: An ablation study removes one component at a time and records how much the result gets worse. The dot plot shows each variant's mean with a 95 percent interval against the full-model baseline, so the components that matter stand out.

explainers.title: Response-surface fit and residuals: how good is the surrogate?
explainers.summary: How good is a surrogate model? Compare its predictions with the truth on held-out points. The parity plot shows overall agreement; the residual plots show the structure that R-squared hides.

explainers.title: Parameter-space coverage (design of experiments): did sampling cover the space?
explainers.summary: Before running an expensive set of simulations at chosen parameter values, check that the design covers the space. The plot shows the marginal distribution of each parameter on the diagonal and every pairwise projection below it.

explainers.title: Optimization progress live panel (error vs iteration + parameters): is the run healthy?
explainers.summary: A live panel for a running optimization: the error against iteration with its stopping criteria drawn, and the parameters against iteration with their bounds. It answers whether the run is healthy and why it stopped (or should stop).

explainers.title: Histogram and ECDF: what is the distribution?
explainers.summary: What does a set of measurements look like? A histogram shows the shape of a large sample and the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) shows a small sample without binning. Together they answer where the values lie, how spread they are and whether the shape is symmetric.

explainers.title: Correlation matrix with significance: which parameters co-vary?
explainers.summary: A matrix of correlation coefficients between parameters, drawn as a colour grid on a diverging scale centred at zero, with the value printed in each cell. It shows which parameters move together and which are independent.

explainers.title: Prediction band with data (UQ propagation): how wide is the prediction uncertainty?
explainers.summary: When a model's parameters are uncertain, running it for many draws of the parameters gives a spread of predictions. The prediction band shows the median and the percentile ranges of that ensemble together with the data, so you can see whether the data fall inside the predicted uncertainty.

explainers.title: Sampling-method comparison (LHS, Sobol, random): which sampling covers better?
explainers.summary: Three ways to choose the same number of sample points in a two-dimensional parameter space: purely random, Latin hypercube and Sobol. The panels show the points; the discrepancy under each says how evenly they cover the square.

explainers.title: Sensitivity bars (tornado) and Sobol indices: which inputs drive the output?
explainers.summary: Which inputs drive the output? A tornado chart shows the swing of the output when each input is moved alone between low and high values; Sobol indices show the share of the output variance that each input explains, with confidence intervals.

explainers.title: Noise-floor plot: is the difference bigger than noise?
explainers.summary: Before claiming that a variant is better, ask whether the difference is bigger than the run-to-run noise. The plot shows every seed of each variant, the mean, and a noise floor taken from the spread of the baseline over its seeds.

explainers.title: QQ plot and residual diagnostics: are errors Gaussian and unbiased?
explainers.summary: Three views of a model's residuals: a QQ plot against a normal distribution, residuals against fitted value, and a histogram with a normal curve. Together they test the two assumptions most analyses rely on: errors are roughly Gaussian, and they have zero mean with constant spread.

explainers.title: Posterior corner plot: what do the parameter posteriors look like?
explainers.summary: After inference, what do the parameters look like? A corner plot shows each parameter's marginal distribution on the diagonal and every pair's joint distribution below, so you see the width, the shape and the correlations of the posterior at once.

explainers.title: Kappa-scale sampling class animation: how do uncertainty classes behave under scaling?
explainers.summary: A scale parameter can move a sampling distribution from deterministic to fully random. Three key frames show the cloud of sampled points at three scales, and one curve shows how the output spread grows between a lower limit (zero) and an upper limit (the prior spread).

explainers.title: Ignition delay against 1000/T: does the model follow the experiments across temperature?
explainers.summary: The standard plot for autoignition data. A logarithmic delay axis against 1000/T turns an Arrhenius-like temperature dependence into a straight line, so slope, curvature and model-versus-experiment agreement can all be judged by eye.

explainers.title: Laminar flame speed against equivalence ratio: does the model match flame data?
explainers.summary: A bell-shaped curve of unstretched flame speed over fuel-air ratio, with experiment markers and error bars, one curve per dilution level. It shows where a model is fast, slow, or peaks in the wrong place.

explainers.title: Extinction strain rate: where does the flame go out?
explainers.summary: Strain rate at which a counterflow flame extinguishes, plotted against equivalence ratio on a log axis, with competing models and measured points. It tests how robust the chemistry is, not just how fast the flame burns.

explainers.title: Species profiles: are the intermediates right?
explainers.summary: Mole fractions of reactants, products and radicals against time in a constant-volume reactor, in the same panel on a linear and on a log axis. The log panel is where the radicals and intermediates become visible.

explainers.title: Ignitability and stiffness map in (T, p, phi)
explainers.summary: A three-dimensional scatter of temperature, pressure and equivalence ratio, coloured by a stiffness ratio and marked where the mixture does not ignite, with the training region outlined. It shows where a surrogate model is being asked to extrapolate.

explainers.title: Reaction sensitivity and flux: which reactions matter?
explainers.summary: A sorted bar chart of normalised sensitivity coefficients next to a Sankey diagram of normalised flux. Sensitivity shows which rate constants control an output, flux shows where the mass actually goes.

explainers.title: Arrhenius parameter scatter within uncertainty bounds
explainers.summary: For each reaction, a bar for the prior uncertainty range with a marker for the starting value and the optimised value of log A, n and Ea. It tells whether an optimiser stayed inside what the kinetics literature allows.

explainers.title: Reaction network graph: how is the chemistry connected?
explainers.summary: Species as nodes sized by flux and reactions as arrows with width equal to flux, laid out from reactants on the left to products on the right. It shows the dominant pathway and the branches around it.
